author: haiku
reason: Document A is easier for a newcomer to follow: its summary, its terms and its single "Each charge" procedure show in one place how the claim row prevents double charges. Document B adds CAS versioning, a freeze flag and a final-pass loop, so a reader has more pieces to hold, and it contradicts itself on what happens to a rollback still running on day 35.

author: haiku
reason: A gives one consistent model: a single rollback path that branches on the origin mode, a clear list of where each piece of state lives, and a "keeps its state in" note on every step, while B repeats near-identical rollback substates in its diagram, adds a no-op "mark paid" step and a self-loop, and leaves the new engine charging during the replay, so its mechanism is harder to trust and follow.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow because each mechanism is concrete and hangs together: the charge key doubles as the provider's idempotency key, gates reset through a rollout epoch, the no-return point is derived from the flag's change history, and reprocessing has a clear job (writing ledger entries marked not charged). A covers more edge cases, such as pinning events against expiry and refusing a second rollback, but it is denser, and it admits its reprocess step may be redundant.

author: sonnet
reason: A is easier to follow from start to finish: it defines "due" and the charge key once and then uses them the same way everywhere, and its reprocess step leads straight into the handover charge. B's reprocess writes to the shadow store, which the switch_back step then ignores, and B itself asks whether that step is needed, which leaves a newcomer unsure how rollback actually works.

author: haiku
reason: A covers more of how the system actually behaves, including crash recovery, polling when no webhook arrives, retries of the claim and release calls, and a saved payment outcome, and it lays out each step's trigger, store and failure handling consistently, whereas B is shorter but leaves several core behaviours (claim failure, missing webhook, charge never accepted) unspecified.

author: haiku
reason: B is the one I would rather be handed: it says outright that Order runs the saga, and it covers the failures A leaves open (a webhook that never arrives, a failed claim call, an Order crash part-way through, the broker going down). Its Rules section states the invariants, which gives a newcomer a full and reasoned picture of the system, though it is longer.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the flow and why the steps come in that order in plain language before giving any detail, its chart separates HTTP calls from events by line style, and its customer-view table and "Rules that keep it safe" summary make the system easier for a newcomer to take in than B's dense opening paragraph and long step notes.

author: sonnet
reason: Every step in A runs on the same mechanism: events published through an outbox, with one HTTP call. Its opening paragraph and glossary explain the whole flow and the reasons for its order, so a newcomer can follow it start to finish. B mixes HTTP and event calls, adds extra recovery branches such as CHECKOUT_FAILED and a declined payment later overwritten as succeeded, and labels some diagram arrows inconsistently, so it is harder to build a mental model from.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: the route is fixed when the row is inserted, the flow runs as seven numbered steps with named topics and tables, and the reconciliation runbook and sweeper are concrete; A is more rigorous, but its NULL-owner claim timing, intent-then-publish relay and 20-hour guard mean the reader has to hold more state at once to see how the system works.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the system more simply and consistently: the route is fixed when the row is inserted, and each topic, loop and check has a name. A newcomer can follow the whole flow and see why rollback is safe. B adds more moving parts (NULL owners routed when a sender claims them, page intents, a 20-hour guard) and contradicts itself: its reconciliation joins the two databases even though its own rules say neither side reads the other's database.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: it lays out today's behaviour, including the retry policy, then follows one notification through numbered steps from Record to Reconcile, defines terms like lease, outbox and due before using them, and has a fuller failure table and a timeline, while A spreads the same flow across separate component lists that are harder to put together.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer the mental model first: the invariants that always hold, a table of the three notification types, and which side owns a row in each status. Its components and rollout steps are split into clearly labelled parts with the reasons stated. A's end-to-end flow is solid but denser and harder to get your bearings in.

author: haiku
reason: B gives an outsider more to hold on to: it defines more of its terms (load balancer, CSRF, TLS, status codes), gives a reason next to each decision, lists the concrete table schemas, works through the sliding-window lockout with real numbers, and covers concurrency across the two instances, while A leaves CSRF undefined and packs its error paths into a dense diagram.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow: it first explains what the app does today, then gives numbered steps for login, protected pages and logout, and ends with one table showing each failure, what the user sees and what state is left; A packs the same kind of detail into a dense decisions table and leaves login storage errors out of its diagram.
